article.title: How to Build a Raised Garden Bed
article.summary: Build a 4×8 ft cedar raised garden bed: pick a sunny site, assemble a square frame, block weeds and burrowing pests, and fill it with the right soil mix.
article.body:
A raised bed warms up earlier in spring, drains better than most yard soil, and keeps your vegetables at a comfortable height. A 4×8 ft bed 11 in deep is a classic first build: everything is in arm's reach and it uses standard lumber lengths.

Affiliate disclosure: some links in this guide are affiliate links. If you buy through them, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. We only recommend products we'd use ourselves.

Safety: call 811 before digging, even shallowly. It's free, and it marks buried utility lines. Don't use old railroad ties or pressure-treated lumber of unknown age for food beds. Wear gloves when cutting hardware cloth.

Steps

  1. Pick a sunny, level spot

    Most vegetables need at least 6–8 hours of direct sun. Choose a spot near a hose bib, away from tree roots, with room to walk around all sides. Keep the bed no wider than 4 ft so you can reach the center from either side.

    Done right: the site gets full sun most of the day, and the bed's center is within 2 ft of an edge.

  2. Cut the boards and corner posts

    Cut two of the 8 ft 2×6s in half to make four 4 ft end boards. Cut the 4×4 into four corner blocks 11 in long, matching two stacked 2×6s (each 5.5 in actual).

    Done right: you have four 8 ft sides, four 4 ft ends, and four 11 in corner blocks.

  3. Assemble the frame

    Screw the side and end boards into the corner blocks with two 3 in deck screws per board end, stacking two boards per side. Pre-drill near board ends to prevent splitting.

    Done right: the frame is square: its two diagonal measurements match within 1/4 in.

  4. Level the bed in place

    Set the frame on the site. Skim off the grass, then dig down under high corners until the frame is level both ways. Don't prop low corners up on blocks.

    Done right: the level reads true along each side, and the frame touches the soil everywhere.

  5. Block pests and weeds

    If gophers or moles are a problem where you live, staple 1/2 in hardware cloth across the bottom of the frame. Then lay plain cardboard (tape and labels removed) over the grass. It smothers the weeds and breaks down within a season.

    Done right: the base is covered edge to edge, with no gaps where grass can poke through.

  6. Fill with a loose, rich mix

    A 4×8 ft bed 11 in deep holds about 29 cubic feet, a bit over 1 cubic yard. A simple mix is about 60% screened topsoil and 40% compost. Fill to an inch or two below the rim, water deeply, and top up after it settles.

    Done right: the soil is loose enough to push your fingers in to the knuckle, and it settles evenly after watering.

Get help if: the site has a steep slope (beds need terracing), you're near buried utilities or a septic field, or you want built-in irrigation tied to your house's water supply, which may need a backflow preventer.

FAQ

How deep should a raised garden bed be?

About 10–12 in suits most vegetables, especially when the bed sits on loosened native soil. Root crops like carrots like more depth.

What wood is best for raised beds?

Cedar and redwood resist rot naturally and are popular for food gardens. Modern pressure-treated lumber is considered safer than older formulas, but many gardeners still prefer untreated cedar.

How much soil do I need for a 4×8 raised bed?

Multiply length × width × depth in feet. A 4×8 ft bed 11 in deep needs about 29 cubic feet, or about 1.1 cubic yards.

Should I put anything in the bottom of a raised bed?

Cardboard smothers grass and weeds, and hardware cloth stops burrowing animals. Skip gravel layers: they don't improve drainage in a raised bed.
